newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-ANDERSON REJOINS JAZZ AFTER DEATH OF HIS FATHER.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-ANDERSON REJOINS JAZZ AFTER DEATH OF HIS FATHER.

text.p: Shandon Anderson's father kept assuring him the Utah Jazz would make the NBA Finals this year. But he didn't live to see it happen.

"From the middle of the season I'd always call home and he'd say, 'You will be there, you will be in the championship game,'" said Anderson, back with the team after missing two games for his father's funeral.
"And for him to say that and then for me to be here and him not be here to share this moment with me, that's probably the toughest thing."

Willie Anderson died last Wednesday of throat cancer, and the funeral was Sunday in Greenville, South Carolina. His son returned to Utah Monday night to work out with the team ahead of the pivotal Game 5 Wednesday that will unknot the best-of-seven NBA Finals.
"It's a real emotional situation right now," he acknowledged to reporters on Tuesday.

Rather than the jubilation his team and all of Utah felt when the Jazz erased an 0-2 Finals deficit at home, the championship series will always be linked in his memory with this sadness, the 23-year-old said.

He would prefer that people not express their sympathy all the time. "I don't want that type of greeting," Anderson said. "I want to move on. I don't want to be reminded of the situation all the time."
He said his coach had it right, yelling at him in practice as always. "Typical Jerry Sloan," Anderson said with a smile. "Treats you like he always does."

The backup guard, whose main duty is to take some of the shifts guarding the unstoppable Michael Jordan, knows the team does not have the luxury of waiting for him to work his way back into a playing rhythm.
Asked if he expects to be yanked from the game if he doesn't play well immediately, he answered: "Oh, definitely."

Anderson, the lone rookie on the Jazz, has played only in their two Finals losses, not the two games they won here. With that in mind, he said, he asked his teammates in the locker room: "I don't know, should I come back? We got something good going here, so I don't want to come in and mess up anything."
Utah superstar Karl Malone put a quick end to that type of talk.
"We're glad he's back, Malone said.
"It is a tragedy any time you lose anybody in your family. We've been kidding him a little bit to try to bring him back in, make him welcome."
"We didn't know exactly know when he was coming back, we were just hoping he'd come back," added teammate Antoine Carr.
"I feel at ease," said Anderson. "The big thing for me was just to get here, get some rest, because last Friday, Saturday and Sunday I really didn't get any sleep."
Anderson, who before every game at the University of Georgia always made sure his parents were in the stands, learned of his father's death in a phone message from his mother at his hotel in Chicago.
"She called me on my voicemail," said Anderson. "I picked up the message. 'call home.' I sat down and hesitated before calling her, 20-25 minutes before I called her."

The death had been expected. "The cancer was in remission about four years. He really didn't have any problems," said Anderson. "Then about six months ago is when it really started happening rapidly."

Even though, "you know it's happening, you know it's coming," he said, "it still took some time to actually grasp it." He made sure to say goodbye, several times. "I didn't know whether I was going to see him again."
His father, who also played basketball when he was young, watched the Jazz's dramatic victory over the Rockets in Houston to reach the Finals. "I got to see him, hold his hand," Anderson said.
"He'd always say 'just play your game, just play hard,'" he remembered.
Anderson was asked about his mother, Dorothy. "I don't think she's taking it too well," he said. "She's going to miss my father." They were married for 31 years.
Anderson's brother Willie, an NBA veteran most recently with the Miami Heat, has never won a championship but is not jealous of his rookie sibling.
"He said he'd love to see me get a ring. I think if I get a ring it won't be just me getting a ring, it'll be both of us."

He also has a family in basketball, he said. During the Western Conference finals, Charles Barkley and other opponents would say to him: "'My thoughts are with you, be strong, I hope your father's doing well,' things like that.
"Just to have those guys say that makes you feel a little bit better. Basketball's like a family. Basically these guys really care about what's going on in your outside life."
